opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about quite a lot. When we started OctoML, the core idea came directly out of the research we were doing on TVM: machine learning compilation, making models run efficiently across many kinds of hardware. We believed deployment and efficiency would become a huge bottleneck, and in hindsight that turned out to be very true, maybe even more so than we expected.

If I did it again, I don't think I'd change the fundamental belief. I might change how we sequenced things. Early on, as a startup coming out of an open-source research project, you're tempted to be very general. You want to support every hardware backend and every kind of model, because that's what the technology can do. But a company needs focus. The market moved very quickly, especially once large language models and generative AI took off. Being a bit more decisive earlier about where the real demand was, and building the product around that, is probably something I'd think harder about.

The other lesson is about the relationship between open source and the company. Open source was incredibly important. It built the community and the trust, and a lot of the ideas came from that collaboration. But balancing what you give to the community with what you build as a business is genuinely hard, and I don't think there's a perfect answer. I learned a lot from navigating it.

Honestly, though, I don't view it with much regret. Going through the startup journey taught me things I never would have learned staying purely in academia: how real users think about these systems, what matters in production, how teams work. A lot of that has shaped how I approach research now, including projects like MLC-LLM and the broader push to make models run everywhere. So I'd make some different tactical choices, but I'm very glad I made the bet.

r001.rationale: The response describes both positive outcomes, such as the value of the core belief and open-source community, and choices it might change, including sequencing and focus.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly I try to be careful with it, because hindsight makes everything look obvious.

If I go back to when we started OctoML, the core thesis was pretty simple: deep learning compilers, and TVM in particular, could make models run well on any hardware, and there was going to be a real market of people who needed that. I still think that thesis was right. What I underestimated was how fast the landscape underneath us would move. We built a lot of infrastructure around the assumption that the hard problem was deploying many diverse models onto many diverse chips. Then the large language model wave arrived, and suddenly the problem concentrated around a handful of model families on a handful of GPUs. The value shifted from "compile anything, anywhere" to "serve this specific thing extremely efficiently." We did pivot toward that with OctoAI, but we were pivoting while running, and that is always costly.

So if I did it again, I think I would hold the technical vision but be more willing to narrow the product early. One of the lessons for me as a researcher turned founder is that generality is a virtue in a paper and often a liability in a product. Customers do not buy generality. They buy a problem being gone. We spent time building for a long tail that, in the end, did not pay the bills, while a smaller surface with a sharper edge probably would have.

The second thing is about the relationship between the open source project and the company. I am proud that TVM stayed genuinely open and that the community kept growing. But I would be more deliberate about how the two feed each other. There is a tension where the thing that makes an open project healthy, lots of contributors pulling in different directions, is not the thing that makes a company focused. I think I would try to set up that boundary earlier, rather than discovering it in real time.

And then there are things I would not change. The team was extraordinary, and a lot of the people and ideas from that period are now shaping how machine learning systems are built across the industry. The work on compiling and serving models at the edge led directly into things like MLC LLM, which I care about a lot. From the outside a company outcome looks like a single verdict, but from the inside it is a long sequence of bets, and many of those bets were good even when the aggregate was not what we hoped.

So I guess my honest answer is: same direction, tighter scope, faster decisions when the ground shifts. And a little more humility about how little anyone can predict in this field over a three-year window.

r001.rationale: The response presents a mixed assessment: it says the core thesis and many bets were good, while also identifying costly choices and lessons about narrowing scope and adapting faster.

astra-6.text:
I think I would separate what we knew at the time from what we learned afterward. With hindsight, you can always point to things you would do differently, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the original decision was wrong. You were making it with the information you had.

If I did it again, I’d want to make the assumptions explicit: what do we believe, and what would make us change our minds? Then try to learn those things earlier. I don’t think the goal is to avoid every mistake. It’s to recognize when something isn’t working and adapt.

r001.rationale: The response says hindsight may suggest doing things differently without proving the original decision was wrong, and emphasizes learning and adapting. This conveys that lessons from past choices can have mixed value.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s hard to say, because you’re always making decisions with the information you have at the time. Looking back, of course there are things I would want to do differently. But I’d try to separate what we could actually have known from what only became clear afterward. For me, the useful question is what we learned from Octo and how those lessons change the decisions we make next.

r001.rationale: The response says some choices might be changed and emphasizes learning from Octo, but it does not characterize the lessons as mixed in value.
